passage: By second period, Jahnavi was curled over her desk, a hand pressed low on her belly, reading the same maths problem again and again. Her back ached and she felt close to tears. When Mrs Iyer asked her to come to the board, she whispered, "Can I go to the sick room?" Pranav snorted. "Periods again? So dramatic." Jahnavi's face went hot. Mrs Iyer turned to him. "That's enough, Pranav. Pain is pain." She walked Jahnavi to the sick room herself. The nurse gave her a warm pack and a quiet bed, and listened. "It's this bad every month, and I keep missing school," Jahnavi admitted. "Then that's worth seeing a doctor about," the nurse said. "You shouldn't have to just bear it." That evening the nurse's note went home, and Jahnavi's mother booked an appointment.

qa.q: What did the nurse give Jahnavi?
qa.a: A warm pack and a quiet bed.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Pranav called her dramatic?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her face going hot, on top of being in real pain.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi most, and why?
qa.a: Being believed by Mrs Iyer and the nurse, and a doctor's appointment for pain that comes every month, so she does not suffer needlessly.

qa.q: What would change if Pranav understood that pain is pain?
qa.a: He might stay quiet or be kind instead of mocking, and Jahnavi could ask for help without dreading comments.

grounding: Shows a student with painful periods struggling to concentrate and being called dramatic, then being believed and sent towards a doctor.

Dear Aditi Ma'am,
I'm sorry I have missed school on some days each month. I want to explain, because I'm worried you think I'm skipping. On those days the cramps are so bad I can't stand up straight, and I feel tired and tearful. When I do come, I can't concentrate, and I've heard some classmates say I'm just being dramatic. I started believing them. Last week my mother took me to a doctor, who listened properly and said pain that keeps me from school is not something to just put up with. We have a plan now, and I'm to go back if it doesn't get better. Could I sit near the door on those days, and could I have the notes I missed?
Thank you for reading this.
Baljeet, Class Eleven B

passage: You want the honest version? Fine. I'm Latika, and from Class 8, for a day or two every month, the pain was so bad I'd lie curled on the bathroom floor. I missed tests. My class teacher said, in front of everyone, "Every girl has periods, Latika. Don't be so dramatic." I started believing her. I'd go to school grey-faced, unable to read the board, too embarrassed to say anything. Then one morning my father, Jagdish, found me on that bathroom floor. He didn't say dramatic. He sat on the tiles next to me and said, "This isn't normal-bad. We're seeing a doctor." The doctor listened, did a few checks, and gave us a plan for those days. It isn't magic. I still get tired and tender. But I'm not lying on tiles anymore, and nobody gets to call me dramatic.

qa.a: On the bathroom floor.

qa.q: How did Latika feel after the teacher's comment?
qa.a: Latika felt embarrassed and began doubting herself, believing the pain was just drama.

qa.q: What made the difference for Latika?
qa.a: Being believed by Jagdish and seeing a doctor, who listened, did checks and made a plan for those days.

qa.q: How did Jagdish see Latika's pain?
qa.a: He saw it as serious, not dramatic, and acted on it at once.

passage: Sunaina, you think I'll call you dramatic for staying home today? Let me tell you why I won't. Thirty years ago, when I was a young principal in Ujjain, a Class 10 girl called Meena kept missing Mondays. I called her into my office and said, very sternly, that other girls managed, so she should too. She stood there gripping the back of the chair, white as chalk, and said nothing. The next month she collapsed in assembly. Her mother told me Meena had been in terrible pain every month for two years and had stopped telling anyone, because we all said it was normal. I felt ashamed of myself. I asked her mother to take her to a doctor, and the school let her rest in the sick room whenever she needed. Meena went on to top the district. So your Sachin Chacha believes you. Now, shall we call the doctor together?

qa.a: Mondays.

qa.a: She was in pain and afraid of not being believed, having stopped telling anyone because everyone said it was normal.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the young principal handled Meena?
qa.a: After she collapsed and her mother explained, he felt ashamed, urged a doctor's visit, and let her rest in the sick room.

qa.a: She saw that telling Meena it was normal had left her suffering silently for two years.

grounding: Shows a student with severe period pain missing school and silenced by being called dramatic, and relief once believed and sent to a doctor.

passage: On the morning of her chemistry practical, Dolma woke doubled over with period cramps worse than ever. The school in Gangtok was a steep twenty-minute climb, and the practical could not easily be moved. She went anyway, pale and sweating, and nearly fainted over the burette. When her lab partner Aditi called the teacher, Dolma begged, 'Don't make a fuss, they'll say I'm dramatic.' The teacher didn't make a fuss. She had Dolma lie down in the sick room, called her mother and arranged for the practical to be taken the following week. That evening Dolma's mother said, 'Pain that stops you standing isn't something to just bear,' and booked a doctor's appointment.

qa.q: What did Dolma nearly faint over?
qa.a: The burette.

qa.q: What was Dolma worried about when she begged them not to make a fuss?
qa.a: She was anxious that people would call her dramatic for her pain.

qa.q: What did the adults do that was right?
qa.a: The teacher believed her, let her lie down, called her mother and moved the practical, and her mother booked a doctor for the severe pain.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt seeing Dolma nearly faint?
qa.a: Aditi was probably frightened and concerned, which is why Aditi called the teacher despite Dolma's pleading.

grounding: A student with painful periods fears being called dramatic, and being believed and taken to a doctor prevents needless suffering.
